_comment: Mutation testing: breaks the source on purpose and checks the tests notice. A mutant that
leaves the suite green is a bug the tests cannot see — unlike line coverage, this cannot be
satisfied by executing code without asserting on it.
Full explanation, glossary and diagrams: docs/tools/mutation-testing.md. This file carries
only the reasoning behind the settings below.
A narrower scope than today's measured 65.69% over everything and 72.22% over covered code,
from 3324 mutants across 100 files in 85 minutes at the concurrency below. Controllers, the
runtime wiring, the tracer, `module.ts` and `demo.ts` have since come back INTO scope (see
SCOPE), so the next run measures more code than that: expect a LOWER total, since what
returns is largely code no unit test imports, and a `covered` figure that is comparable
because no-coverage mutants do not enter it. mutation-baseline.json holds the per-file
record and is the gate that matters — `break` is only the collapse detector.
`incremental` stores each mutant's verdict in `reports/stryker-incremental.json` and reuses
it on
the next run when BOTH the mutated code and the tests covering it are unchanged. Only what
actually moved is re-tested, which is what makes a run affordable outside the nightly.
It buys that speed WITHOUT giving up signal, which is the whole reason it is preferred to
`ignoreStatic`. Every mutant still has a verdict; the verdict is reused rather than skipped.
`ignoreStatic: true` would be far faster still — Stryker reports ~20% of mutants here as
static and estimates they take ~96% of the run — but it drops those mutants from the report
entirely, which is a permanent blind spot over schemas, route tables and module-scope
objects. Speed bought with coverage is the one trade this file will not make.
That file is COMMITTED — CI can only reuse what is in the repo, and an ignored incremental
file makes this a local-only optimisation that looks enabled. `.gitignore` therefore reads
`reports/*` plus a negation for this one file, because git does not descend into an excluded
DIRECTORY: with plain `reports/` the negation is silently dead. See the note there.
A cache can go stale — a refactor that moves code between files, or a badly resolved merge —
so the nightly passes `--force` to ignore the stored results and rebuild from scratch. Fast
feedback on demand, a trustworthy full measurement every night.
A run re-executes the suite once per mutant, so it lives in .github/workflows/mutation.yml,
nightly and on demand. The PR-time gate is `npm run test:mutation:check`, which compares the
last report against mutation-baseline.json in under a second and runs no mutants at all.
`mutate` covers logic this runner can actually reach: `infrastructure` (adapters, the http
pipeline, persistence), `kernel` (registry, events, the auth port and its guard) and every
module's model, repository, service, routes and supporting files.
The bar for EXCLUDING something is high, and it is not 'the tests would not kill it'. An
unkilled mutant is a finding; a file missing from the report is a blind spot, because a file
absent from the report reads exactly like a file with no survivors. Nor is cost a reason: a
mutant in code no test imports is reported NO COVERAGE without running anything, so leaving
untested code in scope is nearly free and is how the report stays honest about the gap.
So the only things excluded here are ones where a mutant could not mean anything to anyone:
- Each module's `index.ts` is a barrel: its mutants ask whether a re-export changed, which
is a question about the module system rather than about this code.
- `src/modules/*/tests/**` is test code, not the code under test.
- `src/app/**` is the Express wiring — routes, security, error handling, telemetry,
workers. It is exercised ONLY by tests/integration and tests/contract, and those suites
are excluded from this runner by `testPathIgnorePatterns` below. So its 126 mutants sat
in scope with no test that could ever kill them: 0.00% on 2026-08-12, every one NO
COVERAGE, not one survivor.
That zero was kept for a long time as a standing signal, and the argument for keeping it
is still a good one — a file absent from a report reads like a file with no survivors.
It was wrong about the GATE, though, and both can be true at once. As a signal the zero
is honest; as an input to `break` it is permanent dead weight that no amount of
test-writing can move, which put a global floor of 70 out of reach by construction
rather than by neglect. Excluding it takes the global score from ~65.7% to ~68.3% and
makes that floor reachable with ordinary work on `src/modules/**`, which is where the
remaining points and the real findings are.
What is lost is a reminder, and it is recorded here instead: THE EXPRESS WIRING HAS NO
UNIT TESTS. If that changes — if `src/app/**` grows a suite this runner can see — put it
back in scope, because then its number would mean something.
The frontend answers the same question the same way for `.vue`, on mirror-image
reasoning: Stryker cannot mutate template expressions, so a score there would imply
coverage nobody has. Both repos exclude what the tool cannot measure and say why.
- Each module's `index.ts` is a barrel and `module.ts` is declarative registration; their
mutants ask whether a re-export changed. `demo.ts` builds the demo dataset and runs
only under `db:seed`.
`npm run contracts:bundle`. Nothing imports one; the bundle they build is what runs.
`testPathIgnorePatterns` above is the other half of the controller decision, and it has two
homes to cover because contract tests do: `tests/contract/` AND each module's own
`src/modules/<name>/tests/contract/`. Those suites drive the real app over HTTP against a
live database; under Stryker they fail in the dry run before a single mutant is tested.
The patterns are REGEXES, not globs — `[^/]+` is the module segment.
`src/modules/[^/]+/tests/integration/` is excluded for the reason this whole split exists:
those are the DB-backed specs that used to live in each module's `tests/unit/`, where Stryker
reran every one of them once per mutant against a real in-memory mongod. `tests/unit` is now
genuinely framework-free (see `UnitLayerIsFrameworkFreeTest`'s Node port), so nothing under
`mutate` is covered from there any more — this pattern is what keeps that cost from creeping
back the moment a spec is added to a module's `tests/integration/`.
`outbox-names.test.ts` is excluded for the same SANDBOX reason as `contract-bundles.test.ts`
below, discovered running a mutation dry run: it reads `emails.ts` source text and regex-
matches `template: '...'` as a plain string literal. Stryker's mutator rewrites every string
literal to `stryMutAct_9fa48(id) ? '' : (stryCov_9fa48(id), '...')` in the files it mutates,
which the regex no longer matches — so the dry run itself fails the case that checks a name
is a literal, before a single mutant runs. Nothing about mail naming is actually broken;
the sandboxed source just does not look like source any more.
`contract-bundles.test.ts` is excluded for a different reason, and it is about the SANDBOX
rather than about the test. That file asserts each committed document is byte-identical to
the sources it is built from. Stryker copies the project to `.stryker-tmp/sandbox-*`
and prepends `// @ts-nocheck` to every file there (`disableTypeChecks`), so the sources it
reads have extra lines the committed bundle does not — the assertion compares bytes and can
never hold. Turning `disableTypeChecks` off is the wrong trade: `ts-jest` runs with
diagnostics ON, so a type-breaking mutant would fail to COMPILE, count as killed, and
inflate the score with kills no assertion earned. Excluding the file costs no coverage
either way — it exercises committed files and `scripts/`, and neither is in `mutate`.
`ignorePatterns` DOES list .tmp/** and .stryker-tmp*/**: those hold the in-memory mongod data
directories, which are live files being written by a running jest while Stryker copies the
project into its sandbox. Copying them is both pointless — every jest instance starts its
own server — and racy: a WiredTiger file removed mid-copy fails the whole run with an
ENOENT on a filename nothing in the project mentions. `run-mutation-tests.ts` clears .tmp
before it starts, which hid this until two runs overlapped.
`ignorePatterns` must NOT list public/**: the sandbox is the only filesystem the tests see,
and tests/unit/db/seed-fixtures.test.ts asserts every seed fixture's imageUrl resolves to a
committed file under public/images/seed/. Without it Stryker refuses to start at all.
`high`/`low` colour the report and nothing else. `break` is the only one that fails a run,
and it belongs at the bottom of the observed band so it answers 'has something collapsed'
rather than 'did the number move'. The real gate is per-FILE, in mutation-baseline.json — a
global percentage lets a strong file carry a weak one. Raise `break` only when a score
SUSTAINS a higher band; never lower it to make a run pass.
`break: 60` is a DELIBERATE EXCEPTION to that rule, kept here anyway: it mirrors the
frontend's own 60 on purpose (both configs were written together and are meant to read as
one pair), even though today's observed band — 28.66% total / 51.57% covered, the first
measurement since controllers/routes/etc. came back into `mutate` scope — sits below it. This
WILL fail every run until real unit coverage closes that gap; that failure is the point, not
a bug to silence by lowering the number. Once a run sustains 60+ on its own, this stops being
an exception and becomes an ordinary floor like the frontend's.
Read `total` against `covered` before spending effort. Far apart means mutants with NO
COVERAGE — write tests that reach the code. Close together means tests run it without
asserting — sharpen what exists. The single percentage hides which.
The ceiling is MEMORY, not cores: each worker is a separate process carrying a full test
runner and its own in-memory mongod, and the machine is in use while a run happens. Lower
this on a smaller machine rather than raising it on a bigger one.
4 on a 32-core / 30 GB box. It was 8, and 8 stopped fitting: measured 2026-08-14, a run at
8 held four workers at ~4 GB RSS each, logged 12 'ran out of memory' worker restarts in the
first five minutes, and then made no progress at all — 1927 of 6040 mutants after five
minutes and the same 1927 three samples later. A run that thrashes does not merely take
longer, it stops finishing.
What moved was the project, not the machine: the domain count went from nine modules to
thirteen and the mutant count from 3241 to 6040, so the same 8 workers now each carry a
much larger program. THIS NUMBER IS A MEASUREMENT WITH AN EXPIRY DATE. Re-measure it when
the module count grows again, and treat a stalled progress line as the symptom.
That 8-worker failure was UNBOUNDED GROWTH, and `maxTestRunnerReuse` below has since removed
it — so the reason 8 failed no longer applies and the ceiling has moved. What bounds a worker
now is the working set of ONE pass, ~2.9 GB, which does not shrink with more recycling:
measured 2026-08-14, reuse 5 and reuse 3 finished the same sample in 4m32s and 4m28s at
23.1 GB and 23.2 GB peak. So divide usable RAM by ~3 GB. On 32 cores / 30.5 GB that is 8 in
principle, 6 in practice, because 8 left only 1.6 GB free and the machine is in use while a
run happens.
4 is kept here as the shared default because this file is committed and the safe number is a
property of the machine: a contributor's laptop is not a 30 GB desktop. Raise it per machine
in `.env` (STRYKER_CONCURRENCY), which is what that file is for.
CI overrides this: mutation.yml passes --concurrency 3, because a standard GitHub runner is
4 vCPU / 16 GB. The safe number is a property of the machine, not of the project.
A run strands one ~200 MB mongo-mem-* directory in /tmp per killed worker (Stryker SIGKILLs
a jest worker per timed-out mutant, so MongoMemoryServer.stop() never runs).
tests/support/global-setup.ts prunes the directories whose mongod is provably gone, never a
concurrent instance's live one — read that file before changing the sweep.
── maxTestRunnerReuse — WHY A RUNNER IS RECYCLED ────────────────────────────────────────
A worker grows by ~470 MB per mutant and does not plateau: measured 2026-08-14, one file,
one worker, heap cap unset — 1634 MB at the end of the dry run, 5850 MB nine mutants later,
linear the whole way. Left alone it exhausts the machine rather than converging.
The cause is NOT this repo's code and is not fixable from here. `bson` reserves a 17 MiB
scratch buffer at module scope, sized for MongoDB's 16 MiB document ceiling. Jest gives each
test FILE its own module registry, so every file reaching mongoose pays it again — ~10 copies
per mutant — and this runner keeps every registry alive because the process never exits. A
normal `npm test` is unaffected: its workers exit and return the memory. Sharing one bson
instance was tried and cannot work; jest routes even `createRequire` through its own resolver
and re-creates `process` and the core modules per file, so no channel survives. The full
case study, including the three-point control that ruled out the database, is in
docs/tools/mutation-testing.md.
So the runner is recycled instead. 5 keeps a worker's peak near 2.8 GB (a fresh runner starts
at ~500 MB and the dry run is not repeated), which is what makes four concurrent workers fit.
RAISE IT if a run has memory to spare — each restart costs a process spawn, and at this scope
that is over a thousand of them. LOWER IT if workers still die. Re-measure with:
npx stryker run --mutate <one file> --concurrency 1
watching RSS against the mutant counter, and treat the number as having an expiry date the
same way `concurrency` does.
